study_sequence.directive: Define a vector space over a field via its axioms (addition and scalar multiplication) and supply standard examples and non-examples.
Define linear combinations and the span of a set, and show how spans produce the smallest subspace containing a set.
Define linear independence/dependence and apply the definitions to prove or disprove independence for given lists of vectors.
Introduce the notion of a basis as a linearly independent spanning list and use it to express vectors as linear combinations of basis vectors.
Connect bases to the idea of dimension, emphasizing that the length of a basis measures size in finite-dimensional settings and motivates later results.
State and use the criterion for a subset to be a subspace, and work typical examples such as solution sets and coordinate subspaces.
State and apply the main results about subspaces in finite-dimensional settings (e.g., subspaces are finite-dimensional; dimension inequalities for subspaces; extension/reduction of lists to bases).
Define linear independence and bases in finite-dimensional vector spaces and explain how to verify whether a list is linearly independent or a basis.
Define quotient spaces V/U, describe cosets, and state the relationship between dim(V/U), dim(V), and dim(U) in the finite-dimensional case.
Explain spanning sets and how vectors are represented as linear combinations of a chosen basis (coordinates), including uniqueness of representation when appropriate.
Define the sum of subspaces and direct sum, and give criteria (in terms of intersections and dimensions) for when a sum is direct.

Define a linear map between vector spaces and state the defining properties (additivity and homogeneity). Provide basic examples and non-examples, and show how linearity is used to determine a map from its action on a spanning set/basis.

Explain how a linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces is represented by a matrix once bases are chosen. Show how composition corresponds to matrix multiplication and how coordinates are used to compute T(v).
Define the null space of a linear map and prove it is a subspace. Include how to compute/describe it in examples and how it captures injectivity.
Define the range of a linear map and prove it is a subspace. Include how to compute/describe it in examples and connect it to surjectivity.

State the definitions of injective, surjective, and invertible for linear maps, and give criteria in terms of null space and range. Include the relationship between invertibility and existence/uniqueness of solutions to T(x)=y.
State and prove rank–nullity for linear maps on finite-dimensional spaces. Use it to derive dimension consequences (e.g., injective ⇔ surjective for maps between equal finite dimensions).
Define the vector space of polynomials over a field (and degree conventions) and use vector-space operations to reason about spans, linear independence, and dimension in polynomial settings.
Treat evaluation at points as linear maps (linear functionals), and use dimension/basis arguments to derive interpolation/existence-uniqueness statements for polynomials meeting prescribed values.
State and use the polynomial division algorithm and related algebraic identities to manipulate polynomials and set up later factorization/minimal-polynomial arguments.
Define p(T) for a linear operator T and use algebraic properties of this construction to prepare for eigenvalue-related notions such as annihilating polynomials.
Connect roots to linear factors, define multiplicity, and apply factorization results to control the number of roots and the structure of polynomials.
Construct the characteristic polynomial, define algebraic multiplicity, and connect roots of the characteristic polynomial to eigenvalues.
State and use criteria for when an operator/matrix is diagonalizable (existence of a basis of eigenvectors), and describe how diagonalization simplifies powers and polynomials of operators.
Define the eigenspace corresponding to an eigenvalue, show it is a subspace (the null space of T − λI), and relate its dimension to geometric multiplicity.
Define eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a linear operator, explain the eigenvalue equation Tv = λv, and show how to find them in concrete examples.
Define invariant subspaces for an operator, show how eigenvectors/eigenspaces produce invariant subspaces, and use restriction to reduce eigenvalue questions to smaller-dimensional problems.

Explain how eigenvalues relate to triangular (especially upper-triangular) matrix representations, including reading eigenvalues from the diagonal and using triangularization to prove existence results.
Define an inner product on real/complex vector spaces and verify the inner product axioms (linearity/conjugate-linearity, symmetry, positive-definiteness) in examples.
Relate linear functionals to inner products by representing each functional as an inner product with a fixed vector (and use this to compute/characterize functionals).
Derive the norm and distance induced by an inner product and apply basic inequalities (especially Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality) to estimate lengths and distances.
Use inner products to define orthogonality, compute orthogonal complements of subspaces, and apply key dimension/closure properties in finite-dimensional inner product spaces.
Construct orthonormal lists/bases (including via Gram–Schmidt), and use them to compute coordinates and simplify inner-product computations.
Define and compute the orthogonal projection onto a subspace and state/use the best-approximation property (closest vector in a subspace).
Define the adjoint of an operator on an inner product space and use its defining identity to compute adjoints and derive basic properties (e.g., linearity and relations with kernels/ranges).

Define normal operators (TT* = T*T) and prove/use their structural properties (e.g., orthogonal eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues, diagonalizability over complex spaces in the finite-dimensional setting).
Construct and analyze orthogonal projections onto subspaces, including uniqueness, formulas in an orthonormal basis, and relations to adjoints and self-adjoint idempotents.
Characterize self-adjoint operators (T = T*) and establish their key consequences in inner product spaces (especially real eigenvalues and orthogonality properties).

State and apply the spectral theorem for self-adjoint/normal operators in finite-dimensional inner product spaces, producing an orthonormal eigenbasis and the corresponding diagonal/operator decomposition.
Define positive operators via ⟨Tv,v⟩ ≥ 0, develop their basic properties, and construct/use the (unique) positive square root in the finite-dimensional setting.

State and use the key facts that become available over complex scalars (existence of eigenvalues, relationship to characteristic/minimal polynomials), and apply them to analyze linear operators on complex vector spaces.
Define generalized eigenspaces and Jordan chains (via kernels of powers of T−λI), and use them to build invariant subspaces and understand the structure beyond diagonalization.
State existence/uniqueness (up to block order) of Jordan form over ℂ and compute/interpret Jordan blocks using algebraic vs geometric multiplicity and generalized eigenspaces.
Define and use the minimal polynomial of an operator, connect it to Jordan block sizes, and use cyclic subspaces/decomposition to derive structural results and classification up to similarity.
Show how a complex-space operator decomposes as a direct sum of invariant generalized eigenspaces, and use this decomposition to reduce problems to single-eigenvalue blocks.

Produce the theorem that every operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space has an upper-triangular matrix in some basis, and demonstrate how to construct/use such a basis to read spectral data from the diagonal.

Define multilinear maps (linearity in each argument separately) and develop the basic examples and constructions used later in the chapter, including how multilinearity interacts with bases and coordinates.
Define alternating multilinear forms, develop the wedge product and exterior powers, and establish the key properties used to define determinants and oriented volume.

Define the determinant as the unique alternating multilinear function normalized on a basis, prove its core properties (multiplicativity, effect of row operations / linear dependence), and connect it to invertibility.
Explain how determinants encode the scaling of volume under linear maps and how they transform under change of basis; connect to orientation and geometric interpretation in finite-dimensional spaces.

Relate determinant to eigenvalues (e.g., product of eigenvalues counting multiplicity) and to the characteristic polynomial in the finite-dimensional setting, emphasizing how earlier spectral results interact with determinants.
Construct the tensor product of vector spaces as the object that represents multilinear maps via a universal property, and show how multilinear maps correspond to linear maps out of a tensor product.
